chapter: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
title: Playing in Ellington's band: Blanton tribute, Hodges and Al Sears
summary: He learned nothing from inside; Duke refused to let him play and never hired a Hodges-like alto player.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: The other thing about Duke, aside from that experience, it was a relatively short time with the band, but what did you come out with? Did you learn anything that was worth learning, or did you see anything about --
With Duke?
Yeah, anything from the inside?
No, because he didn't have any reason.
Yeah.

The music was all messed up, the book was all messed up. And I played with him by hisself. He wanted to have the bass stay up with him when he played. I didn't know the tunes he was playing, I'd just play my best.
Did he ever comment afterward on how you would play?
He commented when -- I asked him to play (unintelligible). He played it (unintelligible) solo, which I liked very much.
: Yeah.
He said, no, no, no, (unintelligible) play it. No, don't do that.
: Why?
I don't know. I don't guess he thought anybody could play it, and he wanted to play his own solo, I guess.
I see. Well, you were sort of like an attribute to Blanton.
That's what I thought he wanted.
: Yeah, that's interesting.
Because, that goes to show you, -- there was an alto player in California named Jack Kelson, who plays it like Johnny Hodges. And I told Duke about him when Johnny died.
: Yeah.
He never wanted to hire him.
I guess he didn't want to sort of preserve the sound because that wouldn't be the original man, so --
Well, he hired Al Sears who couldn't play nothing.
: Yeah.
He sounded corny. And nobody could tell me that anything Duke wrote (unintelligible) Al Sears' work.
: Yeah, right.
